newsitem.title: UK: OPEC oil output boost unlikely after sharp price drop.
newsitem.headline: OPEC oil output boost unlikely after sharp price drop.

text.p: A plunge of more than $3 in oil prices in just two weeks and the prospect of a resumption of Iraqi oil exports dashes any hopes that OPEC may have had to boost production, OPEC delegates and analysts say.

When the 11 ministers of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries meet later this month in Vienna, they are virtually certain to keep their output ceiling unchanged at 25.03 million barrels per day for the first half of 1997, they say.
"It looks certain that we will maintain the status quo. It may have been different if the prices were much higher or much lower than what we have now," an OPEC official said.
The official said the Nov. 27 meeting could end quickly since there is little for the ministers to discuss.
"Short and sweet, that is what we are predicting. It will yet again be a case of wait and see on Iraq," the official said.
A blistering and prolonged rally has taken the price of oil beyond producers' wildest dreams and stunned oil analysts, who had forecast much lower prices.

Fears that heating oil supplies would fall short in the winter and political tensions in the oil-rich Middle East combined to lift crude oil prices to a post Gulf war high of $26.10 a barrel on Oct. 22.

However, mild weather and a steady rise in U.S. heating oil inventories since then has sparked a fast-paced retreat in prices to less than $23. On Tuesday, crude oil traded at $22.90 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

OPEC delegates say the relatively high oil price has vindicated OPEC's decision in June to keep mum about quota busting and not cut output to make room for an expected return of Iraqi exports under a United Nations oil-for-food plan.
In June, OPEC raised its ceiling to 25.03 million barrels per day to reflect a rise of 700,000 barrels in Iraqi output that was expected when the U.N. proposal was implemented.

But that plan to relax a 1990 Gulf War embargo and let Iraq resume limited oil sales was put on hold after military confrontation between Baghdad and Washington after Saddam Hussein was involved in Kurdish fighting in northern Iraq in August.
"Ironically it probably would have been better for us to see the Iraqi oil return now when demand is high rather than still have this uncertainty hanging over our heads," an OPEC Gulf delegate said.
Analysts reckon OPEC coffers will be $20 billion to $25 billion richer because of the windfall.
"OPEC has benefited from the rally. There is no sense in spoiling a good thing," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith Barney.
OPEC heavyweight Saudi Arabia and other influential Middle East Gulf producers are also keen to keep quiet about the rampant quota violations of most members.
Most independent observers believe OPEC is producing nearly one million barrels a day in excess of its output ceiling.

"Since all but three members -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE -- are producing as much as they can, no one is likely to push too hard for any increase," said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.
The latest OPEC Secretariat report predicts demand for OPEC oil in 1997 will average only about 25 million barrels per day -- well below the 26 million the cartel now produces.
